what_its_for: Infliximab-dyyb is used to treat several conditions where your immune system attacks your own body. These include rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis (a type of spine arthritis), psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes inflammation and pain.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV infusion (a drip into your vein) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or infusion center. You will NOT give this medication to yourself at home. Each infusion usually takes about 2 hours. You will be monitored during and after the infusion for any reactions. Do not miss your scheduled infusion appointments.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and the condition being treated. A common starting schedule includes infusions at Week 0, Week 2, and Week 6, and then every 6 to 8 weeks after that for maintenance. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing schedule.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or infusion center right away. Do not try to double up on doses. Your doctor will decide the safest time to reschedule your next infusion.
storage: You will not store this medication at home since it is prepared and given in a medical setting. If you are given any supplies to take home, keep them refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep it out of reach of children and away from light.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine lowers your ability to fight infections. Do not receive live vaccines (such as the nasal flu spray, yellow fever, or chickenpox vaccine) while on this medication without talking to your doctor first. Avoid smoking, as it may reduce how well the medicine works. Tell your doctor before starting if you have been exposed to tuberculosis (TB).
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: signs of serious infection such as fever, chills, cough, or painful urination; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, difficulty breathing, chest pain, or swelling of the face or throat during or after your infusion; unusual tiredness, night sweats, swollen lymph nodes, or unexplained weight loss (possible signs of lymphoma); numbness, tingling, vision changes, or weakness (possible nerve problems); new or worsening heart failure symptoms such as shortness of breath or swollen legs; or signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain.
when_it_works: Some patients start to feel better within a few weeks, but it may take 3 to 6 months to see the full benefit. It is important to keep all your infusion appointments even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you received this medication during pregnancy, your baby should not receive live vaccines for the first 6 months of life. Elderly patients: Older adults may have a higher risk of serious infections and should be monitored closely. Children: This medication can be used in children 6 years and older for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis under a doctor's supervision.
